extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of 37,200 English multiple-choice math word problems from AQuA, densely annotated with operation programs for interpretable math word problem solving.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Problems in the AQuA dataset were carefully annotated with formal operation programs using crowdsourcing. Annotators were given a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments, and they iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper notes unwanted noise in AQuA, including incorrect solutions, unsolvable problems, and rationales that contain few or none of the steps required to solve the corresponding problem.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Math word problems from the AQuA dataset (AQUA-RAT), including multiple-choice options and problem text.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Similar problems were found, numeric values were replaced with generic numbers, and annotations were expanded to cover more problems from AQuA. Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance was used for similarity.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Math problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies. Domains were used to prune the search space of possible operations. Problems not fitting the definition of a math word problem, unsolvable problems, and some noisy automatic annotations were excluded from the final dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers annotated math word problems with formal operation programs by sequentially selecting operations and valid arguments. They were provided with hints for each operation, and after each submission the intermediate result was automatically calculated and added as a new valid argument. Final submissions were restricted to programs using numbers from the problem and producing a final calculation close to the correct numeric solution. At least 2 out of 3 validators had to rank a program as valid. Expert evaluation on 500 problems found 92% of annotations valid.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Alignment validation required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank an operation program as valid. The validation accuracy was reported as 94.64% across categories. Expert evaluation on 500 problems found 92% valid annotations and 87% agreement between expert validation and crowd validation. Automatic annotations from rationales were not included because only 61% passed human validation.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 out of 3 validators for validation; the paper does not state the number of annotators who produced the initial annotation for each item.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automatic calculation of intermediate results during annotation; OpenNMT was used for model training/inference, not for annotation.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to improve interpretability and performance of math word problem solvers and to reduce unwanted noise and statistical bias in existing datasets.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses unwanted noise and statistical bias in AQuA, including incorrect solutions, near-duplicate problems, and noisy categorization based on domain-specific n-grams.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset still maintains the challenging nature of AQuA and the models remain below human performance. The representation language does not cover some problem types such as sequence problems and high-order polynomial problems, and some problems may have multiple interpretations or insufficient context.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for sequence-to-program models for math word problem solving; the dataset is split into train/dev/test and used to evaluate model performance.
